facts.title: Born in the Manhattan Project
facts.text: Americium was first produced in late 1944 at the University of Chicago's Metallurgical Laboratory by Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso. They made it by bombarding plutonium-239 with neutrons in a reactor, building up to americium-241 through successive neutron captures and beta decay. Because the work was wartime-classified, the discovery was not publicly announced until 1945, partly revealed by Seaborg on a children's radio quiz show.

facts.title: Named for a continent
facts.text: The element sits directly below europium in the periodic table, so Seaborg's team named it after the Americas, echoing how europium was named after Europe. This deliberate parallel highlighted the chemical similarity between the actinide and lanthanide series. The naming logic helped cement Seaborg's then-controversial idea that the actinides form their own family at the bottom of the table.

facts.title: It glows in the dark
facts.text: Freshly prepared americium metal is silvery-white, but it is so intensely radioactive that the material warms itself and can glow faintly in the dark from its own radiation. A single gram releases over 100 milliwatts of heat continuously from alpha decay. This self-heating means a visible piece of americium is never truly at room temperature with its surroundings.

facts.title: Inside millions of smoke detectors
facts.text: The most common ionization smoke detector contains a tiny source of americium-241, typically only about 0.3 micrograms, sealed in a metal foil. Its alpha particles ionize the air in a small chamber, creating a steady current that smoke particles disrupt, triggering the alarm. This makes americium one of the very few synthetic elements that ordinary people keep in their homes.

facts.title: A 432-year clock
facts.text: Americium-241, the workhorse isotope, has a half-life of about 432 years, decaying by alpha emission into neptunium-237. That timescale is long enough to give a stable, predictable output for decades yet short enough to be intensely radioactive. The much rarer americium-243 lasts far longer, with a half-life of roughly 7,370 years.

facts.title: Gauging thickness and moisture
facts.text: Industry uses americium-241 in radioactive gauges that measure the thickness of glass, paper, and metal sheets as they roll off production lines, without ever touching the material. Mixed with beryllium, it also becomes a portable neutron source used in oil-well logging to detect water and oil-bearing rock underground. These americium-beryllium sources let engineers see into places no probe could reach.

facts.title: A candidate to power spacecraft
facts.text: The European Space Agency has developed americium-241 as a fuel for radioisotope heater units and generators on deep-space missions. Although it produces less heat per gram than plutonium-238, americium can be extracted from aged civil nuclear waste, making it cheaper and more available in Europe. A spacecraft running on americium could keep working for centuries far from the Sun.

facts.title: Many faces of one metal
facts.text: Americium is chemically versatile, forming compounds in oxidation states from +2 all the way up to +7, more than most of its actinide neighbors. In water its ions paint a palette of colors, with the americium(III) ion appearing pink and higher states giving yellows and tans. This rich chemistry makes americium a favorite test case for scientists studying how heavy elements bond.

facts.title: Not found in nature
facts.text: Americium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount, because even its longest-lived isotopes decay away in mere thousands of years, far shorter than the planet's age. Every atom of americium in existence today was manufactured in reactors or detonated in nuclear tests. Traces were indeed scattered worldwide by atmospheric weapons testing in the 1950s and 1960s.

facts.title: Heavier than lead, denser than steel
facts.text: Americium metal has a density of about 12 grams per cubic centimeter, heavier than lead and roughly one and a half times denser than steel. It melts at around 1,176 degrees Celsius and exists in several crystal structures depending on temperature and pressure. Despite being a heavy, hard-to-handle radioactive metal, chemists have purified it into shiny ingots for careful study.
